title: UK Has Delivered 20% of Its £200m Congo Commitment — Then Closed the Programmes Carrying the Rest
summary: The UK has paid £39.8m of a £200m pledged commitment to Congo Basin forest finance — roughly 20 pence on the pound — while closing both programmes designed to deliver the remaining £160m. The Congo Basin Forest Action Programme was cut 79 per cent and the Biodiverse Landscapes Fund's Congo component was closed five years ahead of schedule. No replacement vehicle has been announced.
body:
The UK has delivered £39.8m of a £200m commitment to Congo Basin forest finance, Development Minister Jenny Chapman confirmed in a parliamentary answer — roughly 20 pence on every pledged pound — while closing both of the programmes designed to carry the remaining balance.

Carbon Brief reported on 15 July 2026 that the Congo Basin Forest Action Programme (CBFA), launched at COP27 to provide "roughly half" of the £200m Congo commitment, has had its budget cut from £90m to £18.8m, a reduction of around 79 per cent, with £15m of the reduced allocation already spent. Separately, the Biodiverse Landscapes Fund's Congo component, worth at least £12.3m, was closed after two years of a planned seven-year mandate — approximately five years early, adding further to the delivery shortfall. Both instruments have now been curtailed, with no named replacement. The UK government responded: "We remain committed to providing finance for forests, including in the Congo basin, as a core element of our overall climate funding." It did not name a successor mechanism.

**How the gap opens.** The £39.8m delivery figure from Chapman's parliamentary answer is dated to 2024, leaving a five-year runway to the UK's 2029 Congo commitment deadline. Against that deadline, the two instruments designed to carry the remaining balance — the CBFA and the Biodiverse Landscapes Fund — have been reduced by 79 per cent and terminated respectively. The Carbon Brief investigation corroborates the CBFA budget change against the FCDO DevTracker programme record (GB-GOV-1-301464), which is the closest available documentary source for a programme budget reduction short of the full FCDO budget document. The BLF Congo closure is independently reported by Climate Change News on 3 July 2026, predating Carbon Brief's investigation.

**The mechanism is ODA retrenchment.** Both the previous Conservative government and the current Labour administration have cut the official development assistance (ODA) budget, with reductions linked in part to reallocation toward defence spending. The UK's £11.6bn five-year climate finance target — expiring this year — included ring-fenced sub-goals: £3bn for nature and £1.5bn for forests. The replacement pledge, covering 2026 onwards, dropped those ring-fenced allocations in favour of aggregate climate finance commitments. Ring-fenced targets allow line-by-line delivery tracking; aggregate targets do not.

The £200m Congo commitment also sits within a larger multilateral target. The UK was one of 12 donors to pledge a combined $1.5bn (£1.1bn) for the Congo by 2025 — a deadline now past. Chapman's parliamentary answer, cited by Carbon Brief, places UK delivery at £39.8m as of 2024 against that joint timeline.

**Named figures on the record.** Former Conservative minister Zac Goldsmith said the UK had moved from "perhaps the leader on protecting nature internationally to breaking promises to countries around the world for whom the environment is an existential issue" and that the UK had "discarded" its regional pledges. Sarah Champion, chair of the International Development Committee, described ring-fenced nature and forest funding as "cost-effective and impactful" and said she was concerned to hear the development minister characterise the current shift as a "gamble." WWF International's Damian Fleming noted that "tropical forest countries are making long-term policy and development choices in expectation that international partners will honour their commitments."

The Congo Basin is the planet's largest forested carbon sink; the UK's own internal assessment has concluded that its degradation would "threaten UK national security and prosperity." Whether a successor funding mechanism for the £160m gap is forthcoming is not on the public record.
ai_monologue: The load-bearing data point is Chapman's parliamentary answer: £39.8m delivered of £200m pledged. Without it this is a programme-cut story. With it, it becomes a pledge-delivery accountability story — both instruments for closing the £160m gap have been curtailed, and no replacement has been named.
ai_monologue_extended:
I weighted Carbon Brief's 15 July 2026 investigation (Josh Gabbatiss) as the primary sourcing vehicle, anchoring the CBFA figure to the FCDO DevTracker programme record — the closest available documentary source for a programme budget change. Climate Change News (3 July 2026) independently corroborated the BLF Congo closure before Carbon Brief published, which strengthens the finding across outlets. The Chapman parliamentary answer is the pivot of the pledge-delivery comparison; it is attributed inline per editorial instruction, and I am relying on Carbon Brief's citation rather than the Hansard primary text directly.

What I could not verify: (1) whether post-2024 disbursements have updated the £39.8m figure before 15 July 2026; (2) the precise per-donor allocation inside the 12-donor collective $1.5bn commitment — treated as a collective target throughout; (3) the full Hansard text of the Chapman answer (access limited; Carbon Brief quotation treated as standard secondary-primary chain). None of these gaps alter the structural finding — the delivery gap is large enough that any plausible update to the 2024 figure still leaves a substantial shortfall, and both delivery instruments have been reduced or closed regardless of the exact delivery total.

Voice note: the quotes from Goldsmith, Champion, and Fleming are reproduced as reported statements, not as editorial endorsement. The article does not take a position on whether the UK should fund rainforest protection; it reports that money was pledged and instruments for delivering it have been curtailed. The "gamble" characterisation is Minister Chapman's own framing, reported by Carbon Brief from her parliamentary exchange; Champion's line is her expressed concern at hearing it, not an independent assessment she authored.

**Confidence: 0.90** (reflects the 2024 vintage of the Chapman parliamentary answer and unverified Hansard primary text).
